title: MODIFYING CLASSROOM ACOUSTICAL ENVIRONMENT TO AFFECT SENSORY BEHAVIOURS AND LEARNING OF CHILDREN WITH ASD

findings.antecedent: noise/acoustics in a classroom environment (qualitative expert opinion)
findings.consequent: sensory response behavioural interlinkage with on-task learning and engagement of children with ASD
findings.mechanism: Noise/acoustics acts as a significant variable affecting sensory processing and learning.
findings.quote: semi-structured expert interviews corroborated the manifestation of sensory response behavioural interlinkage with noise/ acoustics and on-task engagement behaviours

findings.antecedent: classroom or generic environment (qualitative expert opinion)
findings.mechanism: Environmental factors influence cognitive and behavioral outcomes.
findings.source: 4.5.1 Classroom Environment and Behaviour Responsivity, p.94
findings.quote: All the nine participant interviewees underscored that classroom or generic environment played a major role in impacting children with ASD.

findings.antecedent: physical environmental effect (qualitative expert opinion)

findings.antecedent: noise (auditory sensitivity) (qualitative expert opinion)
findings.consequent: disruptive behaviours in children with ASD
findings.mechanism: Auditory sensitivity to noise triggers disruptive behaviors.

findings.antecedent: light (not too bright or too dim) (qualitative expert opinion)

limitations: The present research did not conduct Phase IV of the SCED design.
The study was subjected to limitations of the applied settings, including the school’s strictures and its term semester timeline, which were affected due to political unrest in the country.
The generalizability of the results was delimited by a small sample size and a specific ASD population group.

Some one-to-one learning sessions were conducted outside the designated blue and green cubicle sections but within the classroom bounds due to the ASD student participant’s temporary resistance to a specific setting, which may have affected the results with some variance.
The complete intervention refurbishment involved only the fixed single mode of the acoustic modification aspect, which impacted experiment flexibility.

As the research was experimental and subject to the school calendar time duration, the study was not able to gauge the graduated modification instalment and the flexibility of phase shifting effect correlated to individual participant progress.

The unforeseen consequentiality of the acute heterogeneity of the children participants in the research, including absenteeism and non-attending behaviour, limited the consistency of the number of sessions, sequenced-session and duration for some students.
Data were only collated regarding student-specific sensory disruptive and on-task behaviours.
The important prevalent heterogeneity factor depicted the spill-over impact of tantrums and meltdowns on other children present in the classroom, shifting the normalcy of observations.
The heterogeneity factor was starkly demonstrated due to staff sickness or short leave absenteeism, which impacted the participant’s behaviour and class-peer rapport with the substitute teacher.
